Persuasion Techniques Technique What it means Typical effect on the reader Example Appeal to emotion Using language or examples that trigger feelings such as fear, sympathy, anger or hope Makes the reader feel emotionally involved and more likely to agree “Imagine a child growing up without access to clean water.” Appeal to reason / logic Using logical arguments and clear cause-and- effect relationships Makes the argument appear rational and convincing “If we reduce car use, we can lower emissions.” Appeal to authority Referring to experts, scientists or respected institutions Gives the argument credibility and makes it seem trustworthy “According to leading climate scientists…” Statistics / data Using numbers, percentages or research findings Creates an impression of objectivity and factual accuracy “75% of students reported feeling stressed.” Examples / anecdotes Providing specific cases or personal stories Makes abstract arguments more concrete and relatable “Take Sarah, a student who…” Personal experience Referring to the author's own experiences Creates authenticity and can establish an emotional connection “When I was a student, I experienced…” Rhetorical questions Questions that do not require an actual answer Encourages readers to think about the issue and can guide them toward the author's conclusion “How can we ignore this problem?” Direct address Speaking directly to the reader using you Involves the reader personally and creates immediacy “You have the power to make a difference.” Inclusive language Using we, us, our Creates a sense of community and shared responsibility “We must work together to solve this problem.” Repetition Repeating words, phrases or ideas Emphasises key points and makes them memorable “We need change. We need action. We need it now.” Anaphora Repeating a word or phrase at the beginning of successive sentences/clauses Creates emphasis, rhythm and emotional intensity “We need courage. We need commitment. We need change.” Loaded / emotive language Words with strong positive or negative associations Influences the reader's emotional response to an issue “This cruel and unnecessary policy…” Hyperbole Deliberate exaggeration Makes an argument more striking or dramatic “This decision will affect everyone on the planet.” Contrast / juxtaposition Presenting opposing ideas or situations side by Highlights differences and makes the author's “Some live in luxury while others struggle 1

# Page 2^page=2
Technique What it means Typical effect on the reader Example side position clearer to survive.” Metaphor Describing something in terms of something else Makes complex ideas vivid and easier to understand “Social media is a double-edged sword.” Analogy Comparing one situation with another familiar one Helps readers understand or accept an argument “Managing a classroom is like conducting an orchestra.” Cause and effect Showing that one action or situation leads to another Makes the argument appear logical and inevitable “Excessive screen time can lead to poorer sleep.” Counterargument + rebuttal Mentioning an opposing view and then challenging it Makes the author seem balanced and strengthens their own position “Some argue that…, however…” Concession Acknowledging that an opposing argument has some validity Makes the writer appear fair-minded and reasonable “While this approach may be expensive, it is ultimately worthwhile.” Call to action Encouraging the reader to do something Turns agreement into motivation or action “It is time for us to take action.” Imperatives Using commands Creates urgency and encourages the reader to act “Consider the consequences. Take action.” Word choice / diction Deliberately selecting particular words to shape the reader's perception Can make an issue appear positive, negative, urgent or harmless “Freedom fighters” vs. “rebels” Tone The writer's attitude conveyed through language Influences how the reader interprets the argument A confident, sarcastic or concerned tone Structure Organising ideas strategically, e.g. building from problem to solution Guides the reader through the argument and can make the conclusion more convincing Problem → evidence → consequences → solution What to write in an analysis Avoid simply writing: “The author uses statistics.” Instead, explain the purpose and effect: 2

# Page 3^page=3
“The author uses statistics to provide factual evidence for her argument. By presenting numerical data, she makes her claims appear objective and credible, thereby encouraging the reader to accept her position.” A useful formula is: TECHNIQUE → EVIDENCE → PURPOSE → EFFECT For example: The author uses rhetorical questions (“How can we ignore this problem?”) to challenge the reader and draw attention to the seriousness of the issue. This encourages the audience to reflect on their own responsibility and makes the author's position appear difficult to reject. Useful analytical verbs Instead of repeatedly using “the author uses…”, you can write:  emphasises  highlights  illustrates  reinforces  underlines  appeals to  challenges  encourages  persuades  convinces  evokes  creates  establishes  strengthens  undermines  contrasts  draws attention to  builds credibility  creates a sense of urgency  involves the reader A useful distinction Technique ≠ effect. For example: Technique: inclusive pronouns (we, us, our) Effect: creates a sense of unity and shared responsibility Purpose: makes the reader more receptive to the author's proposed solution 3
